title: World War I: Causes and Peace Settlements
tagline: The alliance system, imperialism and militarism that produced the war, and the Versailles settlement that ended it.

overview.intro: The First World War was fought between 1914 and 1918 and killed more people than any previous conflict in history. This unit examines the forces that made it possible, working from the underlying causes of alliance, imperialism, nationalism and militarism through the immediate trigger in the Balkans, and then turns to the peace settlements themselves: the Treaty of Versailles with Germany, the treatment of Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire, and the criticism that the settlements solved little and prepared the ground for a second war.

facts.label: War period
facts.value: 1914–1918; the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire against the Allies.

facts.label: Immediate trigger
facts.value: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip.

facts.label: Treaty of Versailles
facts.value: Signed 28 June 1919; war guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses and disarmament of Germany.

facts.label: New states
facts.value: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and others created; the League of Nations established under the covenant.

learn.title: The underlying causes of the war

blocks.text: By 1914 the powers of Europe were organised into two alliance blocs, the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy from 1882 and the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain from 1907, each originally defensive but each committing its members to take sides in a conflict between others. Alliances meant that a local dispute could draw in every great power within days. Imperial rivalry over colonies and markets, particularly after the division of Africa, sharpened the same competition, while a naval arms race between Britain and Germany built the fleets that made confrontation thinkable.

Nationalism worked in two directions at once. It supplied the patriotism that made young men volunteer and that allowed governments to present a war as defensive, and it destabilised the multinational empires of Austria-Hungary and the Ottomans, where subject peoples sought independence with the support of neighbouring states. In the Balkans, where Serbian ambition and Austro-Hungarian anxiety met, nationalism produced a succession of crises. Militarism completed the picture: general staffs had prepared detailed mobilisation timetables in which delay meant disadvantage, so once mobilisation began the decision to stop was harder than the decision to go on.

blocks.caption: The four underlying causes
rows: Two blocs turned a local dispute into a general conflict
Rivalry over colonies and markets divided the powers
Patriotic enthusiasm at home and instability in the Balkans
Arms races and rigid mobilisation plans left little room to retreat

items: The Franco-German rivalry after 1871 left France seeking the return of Alsace-Lorraine.
The naval race after 1898 converted a commercial rivalry into a military one.
The Balkan crises of 1908 and 1912–13 habituated the powers to armed confrontation.
Mobilisation timetables meant that hesitation appeared as strategic disadvantage.

blocks.text: On 28 June 1914 the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, visited Sarajevo in Bosnia, a province annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908 and coveted by Serbia. A group of Bosnian Serb conspirators armed by the Black Hand, a Serbian secret society, waited along the route. The first attempt, a bomb thrown at the archduke’s car, missed and injured an officer. After a reception the archduke insisted on visiting the wounded man in hospital, and the driver took the wrong turn; when the car reversed, Gavrilo Princip, who happened to be standing nearby, fired and killed both the archduke and his wife Sophie.

Austria-Hungary, with a guarantee of support from Germany known as the blank cheque, issued an ultimatum to Serbia in July 1914 designed to be unacceptable. Serbia accepted most but not all of its terms, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July. Russia began to mobilise in support of Serbia, which brought in France under its alliance with Russia, and Germany’s declaration of war on Russia and France and its invasion of Belgium brought Britain in on 4 August. Within a week the alliance system had converted one assassination into a general European war.

blocks.caption: How one assassination became a world war
rows: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo
Russia begins mobilisation in support of Serbia
Germany declares war on France and enters Belgium

blocks.text: The treaty with Germany was signed at Versailles on 28 June 1919 and was drafted largely by the leaders of Britain, France and the United States at the Paris Peace Conference. Germany lost territory on every side: Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, Eupen-Malmédy to Belgium, North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite, West Prussia and Posen to the new state of Poland, which also received a corridor to the sea that separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany, and Memel was placed under allied control. The Saar coalfields were placed under the League for fifteen years with their output going to France, and the port of Danzig became a free city.

The military clauses limited the German army to 100,000 men with no conscription, abolished the general staff, forbade submarines and an air force, and reduced the navy to a small force. Article 231, the war guilt clause, assigned responsibility for the war to Germany and the Allies associated with her, and it provided the legal basis for reparations, which were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks. The left bank of the Rhine was demilitarised and occupied by allied forces for fifteen years. Germany was also admitted to the League only as a member in 1926, having been excluded at the start.

Army of 100,000 with no conscription, no submarines or air force, navy reduced, Rhineland demilitarised
Article 231 war guilt and reparations fixed at 132 billion gold marks in 1921

learn.title: The other settlements and the criticism of them

blocks.text: The settlement extended beyond Germany. The Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 1919 dissolved Austria-Hungary and forbade union of Austria with Germany, while the new state of Czechoslovakia was given the Sudetenland with its German-speaking population. Hungary lost two thirds of its territory under the Treaty of Trianon of 1920, including regions with large Hungarian minorities in Romania and Yugoslavia. Bulgaria gave up territory to Greece, Romania and Yugoslavia under the Treaty of Neuilly of 1919. The Ottoman Empire was dismantled by the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920, which was replaced in practice by the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 after the Turkish national movement under Mustafa Kemal, leaving the Straits under international supervision and Greece expelled from Anatolia.

The settlements were criticised on several grounds. The territorial settlements created new minorities even as they spoke of self-determination, since Poland, Czechoslovakia and Romania all contained populations that had been given no choice. The war guilt clause and reparations produced resentment in Germany and a determination to revise the settlement, and the demands on Germany removed the stake a defeated power might otherwise have had in the new order. The League of Nations was founded without the United States and without Germany, which weakened it from the start. Finally, the mandate system allowed the imperial powers to retain colonies under a new name. The criticism therefore is not only that the treaties were harsh but that they were harsh enough to breed revenge and yet too weak to prevent it.

items.text: The Sudetenland given to Czechoslovakia in 1919, with three million German speakers.
items.note: A settlement for self-determination that produced a new minority and later a demand for revision.

items.text: Reparations of 132 billion gold marks fixed in 1921.
items.note: A figure large enough to become a permanent grievance and a subject of political exploitation.

Imperial rivalry, nationalism and militarism were the underlying causes.

questions.prompt: The immediate cause of the First World War was:
options: The naval race between Britain and Germany
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
questions.answer: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
questions.explanation: The assassination at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 set off the chain of ultimatums and declarations of war.

questions.prompt: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles:
options: Assigned war guilt to Germany and justified reparations
questions.answer: Assigned war guilt to Germany and justified reparations
questions.explanation: The war guilt clause provided the legal basis for the reparations later fixed at 132 billion gold marks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was NOT a term imposed on Germany?
questions.explanation: Union of Austria with Germany was forbidden by the Treaty of Saint-Germain, which applied to Austria.

questions.prompt: The criticism that the settlements created new minorities refers chiefly to:
options: The treatment of the Ottoman Empire
The boundaries of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Romania
questions.answer: The boundaries of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Romania
questions.explanation: Self-determination was applied inconsistently, leaving German, Hungarian and other minorities inside the new states.

questions.prompt: The two alliance blocs of 1914 were the Triple Alliance and the Triple __________ .
questions.explanation: The Triple Entente associated France, Russia and Britain and faced Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.

questions.prompt: Reparations demanded from Germany were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold __________ .
questions.explanation: The figure became a central grievance in German politics throughout the 1920s.

questions.prompt: State four underlying causes of the First World War.
questions.answer: Four causes are: the alliance system, which divided Europe into two armed blocs and meant a local dispute spread quickly; imperialism, which produced rivalry over colonies and markets; nationalism, which supplied patriotic enthusiasm at home and destabilised the Balkans; and militarism, with arms races and rigid mobilisation plans that left no room for retreat. Naval rivalry between Britain and Germany is also accepted as part of imperialism and militarism.
questions.explanation: Each cause must be explained as a mechanism that made war more likely, not merely named.

questions.prompt: Describe the main military terms imposed on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles.
questions.answer: The German army was restricted to 100,000 men with no conscription, so that the strength could not be rapidly expanded. The general staff was abolished, and tanks, heavy artillery and an air force were forbidden. The navy was limited to a small force with no submarines. The left bank of the Rhine was to be permanently demilitarised, and allied forces occupied the area for fifteen years, with the period capable of extension. Germany was also forbidden to fortify the region between the Rhine and its frontiers with France and Belgium.
questions.explanation: Four military terms with figures earn full marks; mentioning the Rhineland occupation shows the enforcement side.

questions.prompt: Explain how the assassination at Sarajevo led to a general European war.
questions.answer: On 28 June 1914 the archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife were killed at Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb connected to the Black Hand, a Serbian secret society. The motive was to strike against Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia, which had been annexed in 1908. Austria-Hungary, determined to settle the Serbian question, obtained a blank cheque of unconditional support from Germany and sent Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July with terms deliberately framed to be refused. Serbia accepted most of the terms but rejected one that would have allowed Austrian officials to operate on Serbian soil, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July. Russia, which saw itself as the protector of the Slavs, began to mobilise, which led Germany to declare war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, invading Belgium on the way according to the Schlieffen plan. Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August in response to the violation of Belgian neutrality, which its treaty of 1839 guaranteed. The explanation therefore lies in the combination of a specific act with the structure that surrounded it: the alliances meant that two local declarations drew in every great power, and the mobilisation timetables made escalation automatic once the first steps were taken.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sequence of declarations linked to the alliance commitments, not a bare list of dates.

questions.prompt: Were the peace settlements of 1919 justified as a settlement of a war, or were they a cause of the next war? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The case for justification is that Germany had invaded Belgium and France and fought a long destructive war, and that a defeated power capable of resuming the fight had to be constrained; the military limits, the Rhineland occupation and the removal of the colonies were designed to make renewed aggression difficult, while reparations followed from the damage inflicted on northern France and Belgium. The case against is more substantial in its evidence. The war guilt clause asked ordinary Germans to accept a version of history they rejected, and the reparations figure gave every extremist a ready grievance. The territorial settlements created new minorities in Czechoslovakia, Romania and Poland, so the principle of self-determination was applied selectively and the states created were internally unstable and later susceptible to German pressure. Austria was forbidden to unite with Germany, which satisfied no one, and the mandate system allowed the imperial powers to keep colonies under a new label, which weakened the League’s moral authority. Above all the settlement fell between two positions: it was severe enough to breed a desire for revision in Germany, but it left the German state, its industry and its population intact, so the capacity for revenge survived the punishment. The United States never joined the League and Germany was excluded at first, so the institution meant to enforce the settlement lacked the powers needed to do so. The judgement is therefore that the treaties were defensible in intention but unstable in construction, and that their combination of harshness without prevention produced the revisionism of the 1930s.
questions.explanation: Full marks require a reasoned judgement supported by specific terms and their political consequences on both sides.
